name: getcap
plain: Linux can give a program a single piece of root power (a capability) instead of making it fully root. Examples: cap_net_bind_service lets a program use port 80, cap_setuid lets it change its user id, cap_dac_read_search lets it read any file.

`getcap` shows which files carry such capabilities. It matters in privilege-escalation work: a harmless-looking program with a powerful capability (like python with cap_setuid) can be turned into a root shell. `setcap` sets them and `capsh` explains them.
when: Hunt for privilege-escalation routes on a Linux target.
Audit which binaries have extra privileges (defence).
Understand what a capability string means.

examples.title: Scan the whole system
examples.explain: -r goes through every directory below /. 2>/dev/null hides permission errors. Every line is a file with a capability.

examples.title: One file
examples.explain: May show cap_net_raw=ep: ping may open raw sockets without being setuid.

examples.title: Read the answer
examples.explain: e means effective, p permitted. cap_setuid+ep on python means any user can call os.setuid(0): an easy path to root.

examples.title: Check a running process
examples.explain: The hex values in /proc show a process's capabilities; capsh --decode turns the number into names.

examples.explain: Lets that program bind to ports below 1024 without root.

examples.title: Remove it
examples.explain: -r removes all capabilities from the file.

examples.title: Numeric view
examples.explain: -n prints the root id in namespaced capabilities, useful in containers.

options.plain: Verbose: also show files with no capabilities.
Print the numeric root id of namespaced capabilities.

cap_setuid, cap_setgid (change ids), cap_dac_override and cap_dac_read_search (bypass file permissions), cap_net_raw (raw packets), cap_net_bind_service (low ports), cap_sys_admin (broad admin), cap_sys_ptrace (debug others).
Show your capabilities / translate a hex mask.

mistakes: Forgetting 2>/dev/null and burying the result in errors.
Ignoring a hit because it is not setuid: capabilities are a separate privilege route.
Assuming ping needs capabilities on every system: some use setuid.
Misreading cap_net_bind_service as dangerous: it is usually harmless; cap_setuid and cap_dac_override are the serious ones.
Using setcap on files you do not own in a shared lab.
try: Run getcap -r / 2>/dev/null and list every result.
Decide which results are dangerous and why.
Use capsh --decode on the CapEff line of /proc/self/status.
see_also: setcap(8), capsh(1), capabilities(7), find(1) (find / -perm -4000), id(1), and GTFOBins for capability abuse.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
